question: If I'm held in jail awaiting trial, how long can I be held before I must be indicted and tried, and what happens if that deadline passes?

groups: petition submitted by the attorney for the government
reasserts his right to an expedited trial
inability to meet the conditions of release

gold_sections.why: Subsection (h): a person preventively detained under (b) must be indicted within 90 days and tried within 100 days, extendable for good cause in periods of up to 45 days each; when the clock starts and restarts, what is excluded, and that after it runs the person is treated under the general release section 23-1321(a); (d) sets when the detention hearing must be held; (a) allows a 5-day hold of a person already on release, probation or parole.

The general release section that (h)(3) points to once the clock runs out: its options (release on personal recognizance or unsecured bond, or release on conditions), the bar on money conditions that result in preventive detention, and the 24-hour review for a person held on conditions they cannot meet.
Subsection (b)(3) applies 23-1322(h) to people detained after their pretrial release is revoked for violating release conditions.
Subsection (d) applies 23-1322(h) to a person charged with a crime of violence who is detained as an addict.

Prompt appeal of a detention order, on which the appellate court may 'order the person released pursuant to section 23-1321(a)': the code's own pairing of 23-1321(a) with release, which supports reading (h)(3) as a release consequence.

People charged with first- or second-degree murder or assault with intent to kill while armed are detained under this separate section, which neither contains nor cross-references the 23-1322(h) clock.

Interstate Agreement on Detainers: a prisoner serving a term elsewhere with a D.C. detainer must be tried within 180 days of requesting final disposition (subject to continuances for good cause in open court), or the agreement calls for dismissal with prejudice.

nuggets.text: A person ordered detained before trial under 23-1322(b) has the case placed on an expedited calendar and, consistent with the sound administration of justice, must be indicted within 90 days.
nuggets.quote: The case of the person detained pursuant to subsection (b) of this section shall be placed on an expedited calendar and, consistent with the sound administration of justice, the person shall be indicted before the expiration of 90 days

nuggets.text: The detained person's trial must begin within 100 days.
nuggets.quote: shall have trial of the case commence before the expiration of 100 days

nuggets.text: The same 23-1322(h) clock (and the 23-1322(d) hearing rules) applies when a person is detained after pretrial release is revoked for violating release conditions.
nuggets.quote: The provisions of § 23-1322(d) and (h) shall apply to this subsection.

nuggets.text: The 23-1322(h) clock also applies to a person charged with a crime of violence who is detained as an addict under 23-1323.
nuggets.quote: The provisions of § 23-1322(h) shall apply to this section.

nuggets.text: The indictment and trial deadlines can be extended in one or more periods of up to 45 days each, on the prosecutor's petition approved by the judicial officer.
nuggets.quote: the time within which the person shall be indicted or shall have the trial of the case commence may be extended for one or more additional periods not to exceed 45 days each on the basis of a petition submitted by the attorney for the government and approved by the judicial officer

nuggets.text: Extensions may be granted only for good cause (including due diligence and materiality) and only for the extra time actually needed to prepare for the expedited indictment and trial.
nuggets.quote: The additional period or periods of detention may be granted only on the basis of good cause shown, including due diligence and materiality, and shall be granted only for the additional time required to prepare for the expedited indictment and trial of the person.

nuggets.text: If the deadlines are tolled or extended, the indictment must be returned at least 10 days before the new trial date.
nuggets.quote: If the time within which the person must be indicted or the trial must commence is tolled or extended, an indictment must be returned at least 10 days before the new trial date.

nuggets.text: The detention clock runs from the latest of: the first D.C. detention order after arrest; re-detention after re-arrest, revoked conditional release or escape; a mistrial; a final order allowing withdrawal of a guilty plea; the defendant's reassertion of a waived right to an expedited trial; a finding of competency; a final order granting a new trial; or the filing of the mandate after reversal on appeal.
nuggets.quote: For the purposes of determining the maximum period of detention under this section, the period shall begin on the latest of: (A) The date the defendant is first detained under subsection (b) of this section by order of a judicial officer of the District of Columbia after arrest; (B) The date the defendant is first detained under subsection (b) of this section by order of a judicial officer of the District of Columbia following a re-arrest or order of detention after having been conditionally released under § 23-1321 or after having escaped; (C) The date on which the trial of a defendant detained under subsection (b) of this section ends in a mistrial; (D) The date on which an order permitting the withdrawal of a guilty plea becomes final; (E) The date on which the defendant reasserts his right to an expedited trial following a waiver of that right; (F) The date on which the defendant, having previously been found incompetent to stand trial, is found competent to stand trial; (G) The date on which an order granting a motion for a new trial becomes final; or (H) The date on which the mandate is filed in the Superior Court after a case is reversed on appeal.

nuggets.text: Time for an interlocutory appeal, sanity or competency examinations, periods of incompetency or physical incapacity, and any other time the defendant is unavailable for trial does not count toward the 100 days.
nuggets.quote: In computing the 100 days, the following periods shall be excluded: (A) Any period from the filing of the notice of appeal to the issuance of the mandate in an interlocutory appeal; (B) Any period attributable to any examination to determine the defendant's sanity or lack thereof or his or her mental competency or physical capacity to stand trial; (C) Any period attributable to the inability of the defendant to participate in his or her defense because of mental incompetency or physical incapacity; and (D) Any period in which the defendant is otherwise unavailable for trial.

nuggets.text: Once the 100 days (as computed and as extended) have run, the statute directs that the defendant be treated in accordance with 23-1321(a), the general pretrial release decision; it states no other consequence: no dismissal of the charges, and no separate remedy for missing only the 90-day indictment deadline.
nuggets.quote: After 100 days, as computed under paragraphs (2) and (4) of this section, or such period or periods of detention as extended under paragraph (1) of this section, the defendant shall be treated in accordance with § 23-1321(a)

nuggets.text: That consequence does not apply if the trial is in progress, was delayed by timely motions (other than motions for continuance), or was delayed at the defendant's request.
nuggets.quote: unless the trial is in progress, has been delayed by the timely filing of motions, excluding motions for continuance, or has been delayed at the request of the defendant

nuggets.text: The release options under 23-1321(a) are release on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond, or release on a condition or combination of conditions (the same list also names temporary detention and detention under 23-1322(b), so exactly what (h)(3) requires is a question of interpretation).
nuggets.quote: (1) Released on personal recognizance or upon execution of an unsecured appearance bond under subsection (b) of this section; (2) Released on a condition or combination of conditions under subsection (c) of this section

nuggets.text: A judge may not use a money condition (property forfeiture or a surety bail bond) to protect safety, and may use one to assure court appearance only if it does not result in the person's preventive detention, except as 23-1322(b) allows.
nuggets.quote: A judicial officer may not impose a financial condition under paragraph (1)(B)(xii) or (xiii) of this subsection to assure the safety of any other person or the community, but may impose such a financial condition to reasonably assure the defendant's presence at all court proceedings that does not result in the preventive detention of the person, except as provided in § 23-1322(b)

nuggets.text: A detention order can be appealed; the appellate court may remand or order the person released under 23-1321(a), and must decide the appeal promptly.
nuggets.quote: the court may remand the case for a further hearing, or may, with or without additional evidence, order the person released pursuant to section 23-1321(a). The appeal shall be determined promptly.

nuggets.text: A person charged with first- or second-degree murder or assault with intent to kill while armed may be detained under a separate section (23-1325), which does not contain the 90/100-day clock.
nuggets.quote: A person who is charged with murder in the first degree, murder in the second degree, or assault with intent to kill while armed shall be treated in accordance with the provisions of section 23-1321 unless the judicial officer has reason to believe that no one or more conditions of release will reasonably assure that the person will not flee or pose a danger to any other person or to the community. If such a risk of flight or danger is believed to exist, the person may be ordered detained.

nuggets.text: A person still held 24 hours after the release hearing because they cannot meet their release conditions is entitled, on application, to have the judge who set the conditions review them (this person is not under the 23-1322(h) clock).
nuggets.quote: A person for whom conditions of release are imposed and who, after 24 hours from the time of the release hearing, continues to be detained as a result of inability to meet the conditions of release, shall upon application be entitled to have the conditions reviewed by the judicial officer who imposed them.

nuggets.text: A person charged while already on release, probation, parole or supervised release can be held for up to 5 days, excluding weekends and holidays, while the prosecutor notifies the court or official supervising them.
nuggets.quote: The judicial officer shall order the detention of a person charged with an offense for a period of not more than 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays, and direct the attorney for the government to notify the appropriate court, probation or parole official, or local or state law enforcement official

nuggets.text: The detention hearing is held at the first appearance; except for good cause, a continuance is limited to 5 days if the defendant asks and 3 days if the prosecutor asks, and the person is held meanwhile.
nuggets.quote: The hearing shall be held immediately upon the person's first appearance before the judicial officer unless that person, or the attorney for the government, seeks a continuance. Except for good cause, a continuance on motion of the person shall not exceed 5 days, and a continuance on motion of the attorney for the government shall not exceed 3 days.

nuggets.text: A prisoner serving a term in another jurisdiction who has a D.C. detainer must be brought to trial within 180 days after sending written notice and a request for final disposition, though the court may grant necessary or reasonable continuances for good cause shown in open court.
nuggets.quote: he shall be brought to trial within one hundred and eighty days after he shall have caused to be delivered to the prosecuting officer and the appropriate court of the prosecuting officer's jurisdiction written notice of the place of his imprisonment and his request for a final disposition to be made of the indictment, information, or complaint; provided, that, for good cause shown in open court, the prisoner or his counsel being present, the court having jurisdiction of the matter may grant any necessary or reasonable continuance

nuggets.text: Under the detainer agreement as enacted in the D.C. Code, a charge not brought to trial within its time limit is to be dismissed with prejudice (federal law allows dismissal with or without prejudice when the United States is the receiving State; see out_of_corpus).
nuggets.quote: in the event that an action on the indictment, information, or complaint on the basis of which the detainer has been lodged is not brought to trial within the period provided in Article III or Article IV hereof, the appropriate court of the jurisdiction where the indictment, information, or complaint has been pending shall enter an order dismissing the same with prejudice

deadline.anchor: start of detention under 23-1322(b) (the latest of the dates in (h)(2)); indictment must be returned
start of detention under 23-1322(b) (the latest of the dates in (h)(2), excluding the periods in (h)(4)); trial must commence

maximum length of each extension of the indictment or trial deadline, on the prosecutor's petition approved by the judicial officer for good cause (in force through December 31, 2026; 20 days each from January 1, 2027 unless the Secure DC sunset is extended)
before the new trial date, when the deadlines are tolled or extended; indictment must be returned
after the release hearing, for a person still held because they cannot meet release conditions; may apply for review of the conditions
maximum hold, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and holidays, of a person charged while on release, probation, parole or supervised release, while the supervising authority is notified
maximum continuance of the detention hearing on the defendant's motion, except for good cause (3 days on the prosecutor's motion)

office.value: Judicial officer of the Superior Court of the District of Columbia (orders detention, approves extensions, and applies the release rules once the clock runs)
Attorney for the government (the prosecutor, who must petition for any extension)

answer:
D.C.'s clock covers people ordered held under the pretrial-detention law, including after release is revoked [N3] or as addicts charged with violent crimes [N4]. You must be indicted within 90 days [N1] and tried within 100 days [N2]. The clock starts with your detention order and restarts after re-detention, a mistrial, a new trial, a reversal, or reasserting a waived expedited-trial right [N8]. Appeals, competency exams and times you're unavailable don't count [N9]. The prosecutor can get extensions of up to 45 days each (20 days from 2027 unless the Council acts) [N5], only for good cause and only for the time needed [N6].

The consequence runs from the 100 days, not the 90 [N10]: the judge must then treat you under the general release rules [N10], whose release options are your own recognizance, an unsecured bond, or conditions [N12], and a money bond can't be set so that it keeps you jailed [N13]. That doesn't apply if trial is underway or was delayed by timely motions (not continuances) or at your request [N11]. The law doesn't say charges are dismissed [N10]. Detention orders can be appealed promptly [N14].

There's no clock if you're charged with murder or assault with intent to kill while armed [N15], or held only because you can't meet release conditions, though you can seek review after 24 hours [N16]. Prisoners elsewhere with a D.C. detainer can demand trial within 180 days, subject to good-cause continuances [N19]; the agreement calls for dismissal with prejudice [N20].

out_of_corpus.what: The constitutional speedy trial right, which applies to every defendant (detained or released, and to people held under 23-1325 or on unmet release conditions who have no statutory clock) and whose remedy is dismissal; it is judged by a balancing test (length of delay, reason, assertion of the right, prejudice). The federal Speedy Trial Act governs only cases in the U.S. District Court, not D.C. Superior Court.
out_of_corpus.where: Sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution; Barker v. Wingo, 407 U.S. 514 (1972); 18 U.S.C. § 3161 et seq. (federal court only)

out_of_corpus.what: When the United States is the receiving State under the Interstate Agreement on Detainers, a dismissal for violating the agreement may be with or without prejudice, weighed on listed factors. The D.C. Code copy (24-801 to 24-805) does not include this provision; whether it reaches D.C. Superior Court prosecutions brought in the name of the United States depends on case law.
out_of_corpus.where: Interstate Agreement on Detainers Act, 18 U.S.C. App. 2 § 9(1)

out_of_corpus.what: Dismissal for unnecessary delay in presenting a charge to a grand jury or bringing a defendant to trial; timing of presentment, the preliminary hearing and grand jury practice; and how the courts read 23-1322(h) (what treatment under 23-1321(a) requires once the 100 days run, given that 23-1321(a) also lists detention; how extensions, waivers and excluded time are counted)
out_of_corpus.where: Superior Court of the District of Columbia Rules of Criminal Procedure (Rules 5, 5.1 and 48(b)) and D.C. Court of Appeals decisions construing D.C. Code § 23-1322(h)

version_flags: 23-1322(h)(1)'s extension limit of 'not to exceed 45 days each' comes from section 30(f) of the Secure DC Omnibus Amendment Act of 2024 (D.C. Law 25-175), whose only change to subsection (h) replaced 'not to exceed 20 days each'. Under section 30(k) of that law as amended by section 8(b)(2) of the permanent Peace DC Omnibus Amendment Act of 2025 (D.C. Law 26-52, effective October 28, 2025), these amendments expire December 31, 2026, so from January 1, 2027 (82 days after as_of) extensions revert to 20 days each unless the Council acts again. The same sunset covers the 23-1322(c)(9) crime-of-violence detention presumption, the Secure DC amendments to 23-1325, and the section 30(h) amendments to the 23-1331 definitions ('crime of violence', 'dangerous crime'), which decide who can be detained under 23-1322(b)(1)(A); the code page does not itemize which definition entries section 30(h) added.

The corpus copy of 23-1322 also carries a note that it includes temporary legislation expiring September 11, 2026. That temporary law is D.C. Law 26-81, the Peace DC Omnibus Temporary Amendment Act of 2025 (effective January 29, 2026), the temporary twin of D.C. Law 26-52: its section 7(b) made the same changes, including the same December 31, 2026 sunset, so its expiry changed no text. code.dccouncil.gov (checked 2026-10-10) shows the same subsection (h) text, so the corpus text is treated as in force today.

The code page for 23-1322 carries both a section 45 applicability note (D.C. Law 25-175 section 30(f) is subject to funding; 'has not been implemented') and the Chief Financial Officer's letter of August 5, 2024 stating the amendment 'has been funded' and so 'has been implemented'. The later CFO note controls, so the 45-day limit is treated as in effect.
notes: D.C. has no general speedy trial statute: the only statutory pretrial clock for adults is 23-1322(h), which is written for people preventively detained under 23-1322(b), and is applied by cross-reference to addict detention (23-1323(d)) and to detention after revocation of release (23-1329(b)(3)). It does not cover people detained under 23-1325 (murder, assault with intent to kill while armed), people held because they cannot meet release conditions set under 23-1321(c), or released defendants, who rely on the Sixth Amendment and Superior Court Rule 48(b). The statutory consequence for missing the deadline is treatment under 23-1321(a), not dismissal; 23-1321(a) lists release on recognizance or unsecured bond, release on conditions, temporary detention and detention under 23-1322(b), so (h)(3) is read as a release consequence by inference (23-1324(b) pairs 23-1321(a) with release) and its exact effect is for case law. Release on conditions must use the least restrictive condition or combination (23-1321(c)(1)(B)), such as third-party custody, curfew or return to custody for specified hours. Missing only the 90-day indictment deadline has no separately stated consequence. The only D.C. statutory dismissal-with-prejudice remedy for delay is in the Interstate Agreement on Detainers (24-801, Articles III, IV(c) 120 days after arrival on the prosecutor's request, IV(e), V(c); tolled while the prisoner is unable to stand trial, Article VI(a)). An interlocutory government appeal under 23-104 is expedited (23-104(e)), the defendant is detained or released under Chapter 13 meanwhile (23-104(f)), and the appeal period is excluded from the 100 days (23-1322(h)(4)(A)). The reference drops the earlier nugget listing examples of good cause (unavailable essential witness, forensic analysis, and others in 23-1322(h)(1)) to keep the answer within length. Misdemeanors are generally charged by information, so the 90-day indictment deadline is a felony concept. A child in secure detention must have a factfinding hearing within 30 days (45 days for listed serious offenses), with limited good-cause continuances, and is released on motion if it does not begin in time (16-2310(e)). The 'attorney for the government' is usually the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. felonies and most adult offenses.
